title: Fabriq Developer vs Arcade: Free Tiers, Tool Counts and the OAuth App You Didn't Plan For
summary: Free tiers, catalogue counts, whose OAuth client you use, and Arcade's user verifier requirement. First-party, checked 29 October 2026.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Arcade's free tier is 2,000 tool calls a month. Ours is 20,000 calls. But the number that will cost you a weekend is neither of those.** It is a line in Arcade's production docs saying its default OAuth apps "can *only* be used with the Arcade user verifier, which requires each end user to sign in to an Arcade account that is a member of your project."


*Correction since we first published this page on 2026-10-12: Arcade's pricing page then metered auth events separately — 2,000 included on Free, $0.10 each on Team. On 2026-10-29 that line is gone and the page prices tool calls only. We had built an argument on the second meter, and it is no longer there.*


Read that twice if you're building a product for strangers. The fast path works beautifully while you are the only user. Moving to real customers means your own OAuth app per provider *and* a custom user verifier, which is a route you write and host.


We don't have that step. Your users never create a Fabriq account, and identity comes from the request your own auth already handled. What we do have is a plan boundary and an uneven catalogue floor. Agentic Fabriq's shared provider apps are a paid-plan feature, so on Free your users connect through an OAuth app you register, and Gmail and full Google Drive use your own Google app on every plan because Google treats those scopes as restricted. The catalogue is 511 providers, of which 125 have a live OAuth sign-in, 12 are building one, and 374 have none and connect by credential on a page we host.


We also think Arcade has the better claim on tool quality. It publishes an Optimized versus Unoptimized split and says the unoptimized ones each "mirror one HTTP endpoint", which is a more honest description of most catalogues in this market than the numbers anyone prints.


So: before you write a line, check whether your provider has a default Arcade auth provider, and check whether it's one of the thirteen our end-user OAuth flow drives end to end. Those two lookups decide this.


**Published by Agentic Fabriq.** This is a first-party comparison: we make one of the two products on it, so read it as our argument rather than an independent test. We score neither product and we call nothing here independent. **Comparison checked: 29 October 2026.** Every Arcade claim below links to Arcade's own current pricing page or documentation, with the date we read it; where a figure is not published on a primary source we say so instead of estimating, and where a figure has changed since our first reading we show both. Fabriq figures come from our own[pricing page](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/pricing) , the[Fabriq Developer page](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/developers) , the[Developer Quickstart](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/docs/dev-quickstart) , and the generated provider catalogue in our codebase.


## Overview


Arcade and Fabriq Developer are the two products in this market with the most similar thesis, and we've said so in print before. Both put the acting user in the middle of the call. Both keep the credential out of the agent. Arcade's homepage calls itself "the actions runtime between your agents and every system they reach" and says agents "act on behalf of the authenticated user, never through broad service accounts," which is the shape we build around too.


Which makes the architecture comparison boring, so this isn't one. Our other pages cover that ground:[10 Best AI Agent Integration Platforms](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/blog/best-ai-agent-integration-platforms) and[Composio alternatives](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/blog/composio-alternatives) both rank the category on governance.


This one is for the Friday before you've raised a Series A. What's in the free tier, how big the catalogue is and how it's counted, what you set up before the first authenticated call, whose OAuth client it is, and what happens to your users' tokens. Arcade figures come from its pricing page and docs, re-read 2026-10-29 and quoted. Ours come from our pricing page, our[Developer Quickstart](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/docs/dev-quickstart) and the generated catalogue in our codebase.


**One difference frames all of it:** Arcade sells to the agent's operator, so its free path assumes the user is you. We sell to a product with customers, so ours assumes the user is a stranger who will never hear our name. Neither assumption is wrong, and picking the mismatched one is expensive.


## The Free Tiers, Line by Line


Arcade's Free plan is "$0 platform fee, no credit card required" with "2,000 tool calls / month to take real actions", "Fully managed on Arcade Cloud" and "Community support on Discord and GitHub". Team is a "$25 / month platform fee" then "Tool calls at $0.01 each", also Arcade Cloud only, with next-business-day email support. Enterprise is custom, with "Flexible deployment options on Arcade Cloud, in your VPC, or fully air-gapped" plus "SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and private registry access", a dedicated FDE and account team and 24/7 SLA-backed support.


Note what is no longer there. When we published this page on 2026-10-12 the pricing page metered auth events as their own unit — 2,000 included on Free, $0.10 each on Team. On 2026-10-29 the word "auth" appears on that page only inside "audit logs", and tool calls are the only billed unit we can find. If you read an older comparison of ours that leaned on a second meter, this is the retraction.


Fabriq Developer's Free plan is $0 forever with 20,000 calls a month, unlimited agents, per-agent tool permissions, request logs and live sessions, and the Python SDK,` afctl` CLI and MCP endpoint. Launch is $50 for 200,000 calls and Growth $300 for 2,000,000 ($2.50 and $1.50 per 10,000 included calls), with add-on calls at $2 per 10,000 on either paid plan.


Arcade Free Fabriq Developer Free


Price $0 platform fee, no credit card $0, forever


Tool calls included 2,000 / month 20,000 / month


Separately metered auth events Not on the pricing page as of 2026-10-29 Not metered separately


Hosting Arcade Cloud only Our managed cloud


Support Community, on Discord and GitHub not published per plan


Next tier up $25 / month platform fee + $0.01 per tool call $50 / month for 200,000 calls


The line to stare at is the per-call rate. Arcade Team's tool calls are $0.01 each, or $100 per 10,000, against $2.50 per 10,000 included on Fabriq Launch, $1.50 on Growth and $2 per 10,000 for add-ons.


We want to be careful with that gap rather than smug, for two reasons. Unit prices on an unbundled $25 plan aren't comparable to a bundled $50 one. And the units differ: a Fabriq call is any request your agent makes through us, including authenticating and retrieving credentials, where Arcade's unit is the tool call itself. Arcade's Enterprise tier is custom and unpublished, and that's presumably where a real customer lands, so above prototype volume Arcade's Team list price isn't the number you'll pay and nobody outside Arcade can say what is.


What we can say flatly: 2,000 calls a month is tight. One afternoon debugging a loop can spend it.


## Counting Catalogues, Which Nobody Does the Same Way


When we last checked Arcade in August 2026 it published no catalogue count. Its homepage has since advertised "8,000+ permission-aware tools"; its pricing page publishes no tool or integration count at all as of 2026-10-29. The auth provider list is a separate and much smaller number: 33 built-in providers on 2026-10-29 — Airtable, Asana, Atlassian, Attio, Calendly, Cisco Duo, ClickUp, Discord, Dropbox, Figma, GitHub, Google, HubSpot, Linear, LinkedIn, Mailchimp, Microsoft, Microsoft Power BI, Miro, Notion, PagerDuty, Reddit, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Slack, Spotify, Square, TickTick, Twitch, X, Zendesk, Zoho and Zoom, plus a generic OAuth 2.0 entry: "If the auth provider you need is not listed, try the OAuth 2.0 provider." We counted 34 on 2026-10-12 and 33 on 2026-10-29, and we have not worked out which one moved, so treat either figure as a reading rather than a fact about the roadmap. Its MCP server catalogue, in nine categories from Productivity through Databases, publishes no aggregate count we could find.


Arcade also does something we think the rest of this market should copy. It splits its catalogue into Optimized and Unoptimized tiers, the second formerly called Starter, and describes the difference plainly. Optimized servers "are designed to match the typical data models expected in AI-powered chat interfaces and are subject to evaluation suites to ensure LLMs can safely use them." Unoptimized ones "are heavily influenced by the original API design. Each tool mirrors one HTTP endpoint." Use an Optimized tool where one covers your need, says the guidance, and treat the rest as a complement.


That's the most useful thing in any of these catalogues, because it tells you what a big number is made of. A platform advertising twenty thousand tools is mostly advertising endpoint wrappers. Which are fine. They aren't the same product as a tool somebody wrote an eval for.


Our catalogue is 511 providers and 62,678 catalogued actions, counted from a generated file in our codebase rather than a marketing page, and it splits by whether a user can sign in at the provider at all:


Connect path Providers What your user does


Live OAuth sign-in 125 Gets redirected, approves at the provider, comes back


OAuth in progress 12 Not yet; the credential route is the only one today


Credential only 374 No OAuth flow at all; supplies a credential instead


Of the 125, 87 can run on Agentic Fabriq's own provider app and 116 accept an OAuth app you register yourself. Three quarters of the catalogue has no OAuth, and that is the honest shape of it.


What those 374 are *not* , on the developer path, is work for you. Our developer documentation says there is no admin-entered credential path for external users: every credential, an OAuth grant or a pasted key, is supplied by your user on a page Agentic Fabriq hosts. 448 of the 511 providers reach that page — 444 where your user pastes a credential, and 4 (WhatsApp, Instagram, LinkedIn, Telegram) where they complete the provider's own sign-in, a QR scan or a pairing code. An earlier version of this page said that hosted page supported Notion only; that was true when we wrote it and is not true now.


A narrower limit does sit on top, and it is the one to plan around: the external-user *OAuth* flow accepts thirteen provider values today, the ten Google ones plus` slack` ,` github` and` notion` , and anything else returns` 400 Unsupported OAuth provider` .


**The comparison that resolves this:** Arcade's 33 built-in auth providers against the thirteen our external-user OAuth flow drives end to end, not 8,000 tools against 511 providers. Those are the providers where your customer can run a provider sign-in with no app registration from you, and on that comparison Arcade's list is the longer one.


## Time to First Successful Call


Arcade's quickstart is short.` uv add arcadepy` in Python or` bun install @arcadeai/arcadejs` in TypeScript, then an API key, either passed to the constructor or set as` ARCADE_API_KEY` :


python


```text
from     arcadepy     import     Arcade
client   =   Arcade  (  api_key  =  "{arcade_api_key}"  )
user_id   =   "{arcade_user_id}"
```


Then the pattern the docs recommend wrapping every call in:


python


```text
auth_response   =   client  .  tools  .  authorize  (  tool_name  =  tool_name  ,   user_id  =  user_id  )
if     auth_response  .  status   !=   "completed"  :
print  (  f  "Click this link to authorize {tool_name}:\n{auth_response.url}"  )
client  .  auth  .  wait_for_completion  (  auth_response  .  id  )
return     client  .  tools  .  execute  (  tool_name  =  tool_name  ,   input  =  input  ,   user_id  =  user_id  )
```


A clean design. Authorization is a first-class check before execution, the link comes back to you to deliver however you like, and` wait_for_completion` blocks until the user is done. The quickstart's first example is` GoogleNews.SearchNewsStories` , which needs no authorization, so headline time-to-first-call is a minute or two and time to first *authenticated* call is a different number.


Ours:


shell


```text
pip     install     agentic  -  fabriq  -  sdk            # Python, imports as af_sdk
npm     install   @  agenticfabriq  /  sdk            # TypeScript
```


python


```text
from     af_sdk     import     AgenticFabriq


af   =   AgenticFabriq  ()     # reads AF_APP_ID / AF_APP_SECRET


url   =   await     af  .  initiate_connection  (  request  ,   provider  =  "gmail"  )     # in your handler
return     redirect  (  url  )
```


python


```text
async     with     await     af  .  for_user  (  request  )   as     session  :
tools   =   await     session  .  get_tools  ()
result   =   await     session  .  call_tool  (  "google_gmail_list_messages"  , {  "max_results"  :   5  })
```


Register an agent in the console, get an app ID and a one-time app secret, set them as` AF_APP_ID` and` AF_APP_SECRET` , then two calls. The argument is the request, not a user id, because identity is read from the session your own auth already established. That's the sharpest API difference between us: Arcade's` user_id` is a string you choose and pass on every call, ours is derived from the request. We prefer ours because no agent can get a user-id parameter wrong and send somebody else's mail. Arcade's is more flexible if your caller isn't an HTTP request at all.


**Figure 1 — Both reach a first call in minutes. The branch that matters is the one hanging off the authorization step, where Arcade's default app pulls your end user into an Arcade account.**


Tokens on our side last 900 seconds by default with a hard ceiling of one hour, and the Python client re-mints 60 seconds before expiry, so calling` for_user` per request is the intended pattern rather than waste. For model-driven code the session converts the list with` to_openai_tools()` ,` to_anthropic_tools()` or` to_langchain_tools()` .


## The Verifier Problem


This is the section to read if you read nothing else, and it's the one that isn't on anybody's pricing page.


Arcade does provide default OAuth credentials, generously. Its Microsoft page says Arcade Cloud "provides a default Microsoft auth provider so you can try the Arcade Microsoft MCP servers without registering your own app", and Discord's says Arcade Cloud "includes a default Discord auth provider, so you can start without any configuration." Each carries per-provider caveats worth reading: the Microsoft default supports work and school accounts only.


Two costs come with any default, both documented. On the consent screen, "your users will see the Arcade brand (name and logo) on the auth screen and your authentications will share any rate limits from those providers with other Arcade customers." The harder one is in the production guidance: the default OAuth apps "can *only* be used with the Arcade user verifier, which requires each end user to sign in to an Arcade account that is a member of your project." That "ties end-user authorization to project membership, which is why the default OAuth apps are intended for development and single-tenant use."


For a multi-user production app the docs tell you to add your own OAuth app credentials "and pair them with a custom user verifier, so your end users are verified by your app rather than by project membership." Two pieces of work: a provider project per integration, plus a verification route you write and host.


There is no verifier to build on our side, and no Fabriq account for your customer: they approve on a consent page we host with no sign-up. Our own asterisk is the plan, not the verifier. Agentic Fabriq's shared provider apps cover non-restricted scopes on Launch or Growth after a one-time attestation; on the Free plan your users connect through an OAuth app you register; and Gmail and full Google Drive are restricted scopes under Google's policy, so those always go through your own Google app on every plan. If Gmail is the integration your product is built on, you file for Google verification either way. Every token records an` auth_level` saying how strongly the user was proven:` app_asserted` by default,` app_signed` if you sign a 60-second EdDSA assertion with a private key we never hold,` user_present` if a human just completed a connection and we witnessed it.


**Figure 2 — The decision tree per provider. Arcade's two yes-branches lead to very different amounts of work, and the split is multi-user versus single-tenant rather than free versus paid.**


Arcade Fabriq Developer


Default OAuth app Yes, with per-provider caveats Yes on a paid plan; Free is bring-your-own


Branding on consent Arcade's, on a default app Ours, on our shared apps


Rate limits on a default app "share any rate limits from those providers with other Arcade customers" Shared across our customers too


End user needs a platform account Yes, with a default app No, on any plan


Multi-user production Own app + custom verifier No verifier; our shared apps on a paid plan


Gmail / full Google Drive Default Google provider available Your own Google app on every plan


The catch Verifier work before real users 13 providers on the end-user OAuth path


## Who Holds the Token When the Call Goes Out


Both of us keep the secret away from the model the same way: the credential is attached server-side and the agent gets a result. Arcade's docs put it as "Arcade remembers the user's authorization tokens, so you don't have to", and on the tool-building side, "LLMs and MCP clients cannot see or access your OAuth tokens."


There's one real difference, and it cuts for or against Arcade depending on what you're building. Arcade will give your server the raw token on request. Start an authorization with` client.auth.start(user_id=..., provider="google", scopes=\[...\])` , wait for it, and` auth_response.context.token` is the third-party access token, which you can hand to a provider SDK and call the API yourself. Inside a custom tool,` context.get_auth_token_or_empty()` does the same job.


A genuinely useful escape hatch. It also means the token's blast radius is a per-call-site decision rather than a property of the platform, and once it's in your process it's in your logs, your traces and whatever your error reporter serialises.


On our side,` for_user` mints a short-lived, user-scoped token and returns a session whose identity is already baked in, so no method on it takes a user id. The provider credential lives in a vault at a path derived from the organization, agent, external user, tool and connection id, never in a database column or a response body. The agent gets a session, never the secret, and there's no` context.token` equivalent.


Fabriq gateway gateway computes: user's scopes INTERSECT agent's scopes gateway --fetch by reference--> Vault --access token--> gateway gateway --authorized request--> Provider API --response--> gateway gateway --result only--> your backend. The credential never leaves the gateway. -->


**Figure 3 — Our call path. The effective tool list is the intersection of the user's scopes and the agent's, so a broadly scoped agent acting for a narrowly scoped user gets the narrow set.**


The intersection is the piece a prototype doesn't notice and a second customer does. An agent declares the scopes it may ever ask for when you register it; a user grants what they grant; the effective list is the overlap. Arcade describes a comparable model, saying authorization "is delegated, so the agent acts as its user and never past its own scope," which we'd read as the same idea arrived at independently.


What neither of us should be assumed to do is kill the grant at the provider. Disconnecting clears the grant we store, and if you need the token dead at Google you call Google's revocation endpoint yourself. We'd ask Arcade the same question rather than guess.

## Where Arcade Is the Better Pick


Arcade is the competitor whose thesis we respect most, so this list is longer than it would be for anyone else.


**You want the raw token.**` auth_response.context.token` has no equivalent in our external-user flow. If your product is mostly your own code calling provider SDKs and you want managed OAuth under it rather than a tool-calling layer over it, Arcade is built for that and we aren't.


**You need to run it yourself.** Arcade's Enterprise tier runs in your VPC or fully air-gapped. If your first customer is a hospital or a bank, that line ends the evaluation.


**Your providers are in its 33 and not in the thirteen our end-user OAuth flow drives.** Atlassian, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Zendesk, HubSpot, Linear, Figma and Miro all have built-in Arcade auth providers. Several of those are in our 511-provider catalogue, but through the credentials page rather than a provider sign-in, which is a different product experience for your customer.


**You care about tool quality over tool count.** The Optimized tier is subject to evaluation suites. We don't publish an equivalent distinction, and pretending otherwise is the kind of claim this page exists to avoid.


**You're single-tenant anyway.** If the agent acts for your own team, the verifier requirement isn't a cost, it's just how your users sign in, and you get the fast path with none of the production work.


## Which to Choose


**Choose Fabriq Developer when** your end customers must never see a third party's name and must never create an account anywhere but your product; when you want identity derived from the request your own auth already established rather than a` user_id` string your code passes on every call; when a free tier ten times larger on calls matters at prototype stage; when you want no verifier route to write and host before launch; or when you want the provider credential to have no retrieval path at all, so it cannot end up in your logs by accident.[Fabriq Developer](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/developers) and the[Developer Quickstart](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/docs/dev-quickstart) are the two pages to read next, in that order.


**Consider Arcade when** you need the raw token in your own process —` auth_response.context.token` has no equivalent in our external-user flow, and if your product is mostly your own code calling provider SDKs, that is the right shape and ours is not. Also when you need a VPC or air-gapped deployment, which Arcade publishes and we don't; when your providers are among its 33 built-ins; when you want more first-party framework adapters than our two SDKs offer; or when the agent acts for your own team, in which case the verifier requirement is just how your users sign in and you get the fast path for free.


If you want the governance argument instead, the[agent access control taxonomy](https://agenticfabriq.github.io/agent-access-control-taxonomy/) sets out the nine dimensions, credential model and delegation model among them, that a security review eventually asks about.


## Frequently Asked Questions


**Is Arcade free?** Yes. As of 2026-10-29 the Free plan is a $0 platform fee with no credit card and 2,000 tool calls a month on Arcade Cloud, with community support on Discord and GitHub. Team is a $25 monthly platform fee plus "Tool calls at $0.01 each". The separately metered auth event that appeared on the page on 2026-10-12 is no longer there.


**Is Fabriq Developer free?** Yes. The Free plan is $0 forever with 20,000 calls a month, unlimited agents, per-agent tool permissions, request logs and live sessions, and the SDK, CLI and MCP endpoint.


**How many tools does Arcade have?** Its homepage says "8,000+ permission-aware tools", and its auth provider page listed 33 built-in providers plus a generic OAuth 2.0 option on 2026-10-29. Its pricing page publishes no count, and we found no published aggregate count of MCP servers in its catalogue.


**How many integrations does Fabriq Developer have?** 511 providers and 62,678 catalogued actions, from the generated catalogue in our codebase on 2026-10-29: 125 with a live OAuth sign-in, 12 with one in progress, 374 that connect by credential. The end-user OAuth flow accepts thirteen provider values today; 448 providers reach the hosted credentials page your user fills in.


**Do I need my own OAuth app to use Arcade?** Not in development, for the many providers with a default. But the default apps work only with Arcade's user verifier, which requires each end user to have an Arcade account in your project, so multi-user production needs your own app and a custom verifier.


**Do I need my own OAuth app to use Fabriq Developer?** It depends on the plan and the scope, and there is no verifier to build either way. On Free, yes: your users connect through your own OAuth app. On Launch or Growth, our shared apps cover non-restricted scopes after a one-time attestation. Gmail and full Google Drive are restricted scopes under Google's policy and use your own Google app on every plan.


**Do my users need an Arcade account?** On a default Arcade OAuth app, yes, per its production docs. With your own OAuth app and a custom verifier, no. With us, no.


**Which is cheaper, Arcade or Fabriq Developer?** On list prices, we are: 20,000 free calls against 2,000, then $2.50 per 10,000 included on Launch against $0.01 per tool call on Arcade Team. Two caveats that matter more than the arithmetic: the units differ, because a Fabriq call includes authenticating and retrieving credentials where Arcade's is the tool call itself, and Arcade's Enterprise pricing is unpublished, so above prototype volume nobody outside Arcade can answer this.


**Can I get the user's access token out of either platform?** Out of Arcade, yes:` auth_response.context.token` after` client.auth.start` , or` context.get_auth_token_or_empty()` inside a tool. Out of our external-user flow, no.


## Conclusion


We think Arcade is the closest thing to us in this market, and the free tiers aren't where the difference shows up. Ten times the calls is a real advantage for us and a small one, because both numbers are prototype numbers and both plans exist to get you to a paid one.


The difference shows up at the user verifier. Arcade's defaults are built for an operator running an agent for themselves or their own company, and its docs say so: development and single-tenant use. Ours are built for a product whose users are strangers. If you're the first kind of team, Arcade's fast path is genuinely fast and you'll never pay the verifier cost. If you're the second, you'll pay it right before launch, which is the worst week to find a new project in your backlog.


Against that, our catalogue floor is uneven and our shared provider apps need a paid plan, and we'd rather you heard both here. Check your four providers against Arcade's 33 built-ins and the thirteen our end-user OAuth flow drives before you write anything, and let that lookup decide rather than a tool count on either homepage.


**The question to ask both of us:** what do I have to register, host or verify before a stranger can connect their own account? Arcade answers that honestly in its docs, which is more than most of this market does, and the answer is longer than its quickstart suggests.
